evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs
We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015)
Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)
visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information)
Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.
Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Gil et al. (2016) introduces the concept of the Geoscience Paper of the Future, with a best practice requiring authors to make data, software, and methods openly accessible, citable, and well-documented.
To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and
focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties

Advancements in how we disseminate information should be incorporated into hydrologic modeling frameworks by including tools that will document and publish the computational workflow as well as all the associated digital objects

It is suspected that reproducibility and scientific provenance (i.e., a digital record of what data and methods were used to produce the results and conclusions) will be a key review criterion for future geoscience publications (Gil et al. 2016).

evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)

and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)

evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs
We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015)
Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)
visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information)
Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.
Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Gil et al. (2016) introduces the concept of the Geoscience Paper of the Future, with a best practice requiring authors to make data, software, and methods openly accessible, citable, and well-documented.
To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and
focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties

Advancements in how we disseminate information should be incorporated into hydrologic modeling frameworks by including tools that will document and publish the computational workflow as well as all the associated digital objects

It is suspected that reproducibility and scientific provenance (i.e., a digital record of what data and methods were used to produce the results and conclusions) will be a key review criterion for future geoscience publications (Gil et al. 2016).

While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.

Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)

evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs
We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015)
Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)
visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information)
Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.
Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Gil et al. (2016) introduces the concept of the Geoscience Paper of the Future, with a best practice requiring authors to make data, software, and methods openly accessible, citable, and well-documented.
To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and
focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties

Advancements in how we disseminate information should be incorporated into hydrologic modeling frameworks by including tools that will document and publish the computational workflow as well as all the associated digital objects

While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)

and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.

evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs

Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)
visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information)
Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.

A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

evidenceSpans.evidenceText: Difficulties frequently arise in model performance evaluation due to multiple interpretations of output or data products, differing mathematical descriptions of underlying processes, and uncertainties present in the input and parameter datasets
While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC)
Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020)
and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017)
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.
The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs
We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015)
Consequently, models are calibrated using objective functions (e.g., Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency [NSE], root mean squared error [RMSE], peak discharge)
visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information)
Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.
Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Gil et al. (2016) introduces the concept of the Geoscience Paper of the Future, with a best practice requiring authors to make data, software, and methods openly accessible, citable, and well-documented.
To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and
focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties

Advancements in how we disseminate information should be incorporated into hydrologic modeling frameworks by including tools that will document and publish the computational workflow as well as all the associated digital objects

While sensitivity analyses have been implemented across a variety of hydrologic models, a comprehensive and adaptable methodology has yet to be adopted in common practice.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.
Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).

Provided by Fellows of the NWC Innovators Program: Summer Institute 2019, the HBV and TOPMODEL case studies illustrated the workflow for different model configurations, outputs, parameter sets and number of objective functions.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.

Conceptual and mathematical models are often used to represent complex and unconstrained hydrologic environments (Neuman 2003).
Model parameter values for numerical calculations are often not a direct physical interpretation and can rarely be measured in the field.
Previous studies have called for the adoption of reproducibility and transparency within hydrology to add credibility to scientific claims.
A recent study by Stagge et al. (2019) found low reproducibility (5.6% of total sampled articles) in research published in 2017 from six hydrology and water resources journals.

Gil et al. (2016) introduces the concept of the Geoscience Paper of the Future, with a best practice requiring authors to make data, software, and methods openly accessible, citable, and well-documented.
To effectively model hydrology, it is necessary to understand how the model output is impacted by each parameter and
focus model calibration on decreasing the uncertainties of more influential parameters.

The hydrologic modeling community needs common frameworks organizing the development of open source, multicriteria approaches that are reproducible, adaptable, and transferable for evaluating model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties
